metadata.title: Comparing the Similarities and Differences of PISA 2003 and TIMSS (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The working paper compares PISA 2003 mathematics and TIMSS 2003 Grade 8 mathematics using published country-level results and additional crosswalks between frameworks (e.g., mapping PISA items to TIMSS content/cognitive domains). It discusses the underlying survey designs of both assessments: both use two-stage stratified sampling with PPS school selection, and both estimate achievement using IRT-based scaling with plausible values and replication methods for standard errors (TIMSS jackknife; PISA balanced repeated replication). However, the paper itself does not report an analyst-specific microdata workflow (e.g., which student weight variable from the international database was applied) and instead focuses on methodological comparison and regression analyses at the country level. Therefore, the paper should be treated as using already-produced international estimates rather than re-estimating weighted student-level models from raw microdata; analysts replicating the work would need to apply the official PISA/TIMSS complex-sample weights and PV replication procedures when working with microdata.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is a methodological comparison and country-level explanatory analysis using published PISA and TIMSS results (e.g., country mean scores, standard deviations, and indices derived from content balance). The dependent variables in the paper are not individual student plausible-value achievement outcomes being re-estimated from microdata; instead, the analysis relies on already scaled and reported country statistics and constructed indices. As a result, plausible-value handling and missing-data handling for student-level PV datasets are not applicable in the sense of the paper’s own estimation workflow, and the paper does not document a microdata missing-data strategy.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The paper uses PISA 2003 mathematics and TIMSS 2003 mathematics results for comparison, with the main quantitative country-level comparisons focused on the subset of countries/regions that participated in both surveys (22 countries/regions). It explicitly notes that England is included for illustration but does not meet required response-rate/technical participation requirements in PISA and therefore its mean-score comparability is limited. For the regression-based explanations, the analysis is conducted on the 22-country set (with England treated as non-comparable for some interpretations), using country mean scores and constructed indices (e.g., content advantage index) derived from the framework alignment.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper compares PISA 2003 mathematics (OECD; age-based, grades 7+) and TIMSS 2003 mathematics (IEA; Grade 8 cohort) by contrasting survey methodology, mathematics frameworks, and item/test characteristics. It explains differences in country rankings using country-level regression analyses that relate PISA–TIMSS gaps to (i) differences in content balance between the two assessments (PISA’s item distribution across TIMSS content domains) and (ii) differences in population definitions, operationalized via age at TIMSS testing and an estimated number of years of schooling at PISA testing. The paper also examines reading load as an additional predictor of PISA mathematics differences and reports high explanatory power for combined predictors (e.g., up to 97% variance explained in predicting PISA mathematics country means). Beyond achievement, it compares gender differences and attitudinal indices (self-confidence and motivation) across the two surveys, finding stronger agreement for attitudes than for achievement gender gaps. The key implication is that cross-survey comparisons must account for framework alignment, sampling definitions, and test composition; otherwise, apparent performance differences may reflect measurement design rather than true differences in mathematics proficiency.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD working paper focused on methodological comparison and country-level explanatory regression using published PISA/TIMSS results rather than training/evaluating machine-learning models on student-level microdata. Consequently, there are no distinct ML target variables with predictive performance metrics to tabulate, and the schema’s main_findings and confounders_identified (as ML predictors) are intentionally left empty. The paper also does not provide a microdata-based missing-data or PV re-estimation protocol, because it relies on already scaled and reported international results and constructed indices at the country level.
